questions.q:
The table shows the shoe sizes of 25 students.
Shoe size:  4 | 5 | 6 | 7
Frequency:  3 | 7 | 9 | 6
(a) Write down the mode. [1]
(b) Find the median. [1]
questions.model:
(a) Size 6 has the highest frequency (9), so the mode is 6.
(b) The median is the 13th value. Cumulative frequencies: 3, 10, 19, … so the 13th value is size 6.
questions.tip: The mode is the size, not the frequency: '9' scores 0.

questions.q:
A scatter diagram shows the outside temperature (°C) and the number of hot drinks sold at a café on 12 days. As the temperature increases, fewer hot drinks are sold.
(a) What type of correlation does the scatter diagram show? [1]
(b) A line of best fit is drawn. Explain why using it to estimate the sales on a day when the temperature is 40 °C may not be reliable, when the data only covers temperatures from 5 °C to 25 °C. [1]
ms: (b) B1: 40 °C is outside the range of the data (extrapolation), so the pattern may not continue
questions.model:
(a) Negative correlation.
(b) 40 °C is outside the range of the data, so this would be extrapolation: the trend may not continue beyond 25 °C.
questions.tip: Interpret correlation in context and avoid saying one thing 'causes' the other.

questions.q:
The heights, h cm, of 40 plants are shown in the table.
Height (h cm)       Frequency
140 < h ≤ 150          6
150 < h ≤ 160         14
160 < h ≤ 170         15
170 < h ≤ 180          5
Calculate an estimate of the mean height.
questions.tip: Divide by the total frequency (40), not by the number of groups (4).

questions.q:
The ages, a years, of some people at a park are shown in the table.
Age (a years)    Frequency
0 < a ≤ 10          12
10 < a ≤ 15         20
15 < a ≤ 25          ?
25 < a ≤ 40         18
(a) Calculate the frequency densities for the classes 0 < a ≤ 10, 10 < a ≤ 15 and 25 < a ≤ 40. [2]
(b) On the histogram, the bar for 15 < a ≤ 25 has height 3.5. Find the frequency for this class. [1]
(c) Estimate the number of people aged between 20 and 30 years. [2]
questions.model:
(a) Frequency density = frequency ÷ class width.
12 ÷ 10 = 1.2, 20 ÷ 5 = 4, 18 ÷ 15 = 1.2.
(b) Frequency = 3.5 × 10 = 35.
(c) 20 to 25 is half of the class 15–25: 35 ÷ 2 = 17.5.
25 to 30 is 5/15 of the class 25–40: 18 × 5/15 = 6.
Estimate = 17.5 + 6 = 23.5 (about 23 or 24 people).
questions.tip: In a histogram the area of a bar, not its height, represents the frequency.

questions.q:
The masses, m grams, of 80 apples are shown in the table.
Mass (m g)          Frequency
80 < m ≤ 100           8
100 < m ≤ 120         18
120 < m ≤ 140         30
140 < m ≤ 160         16
160 < m ≤ 180          8
(a) Complete a cumulative frequency table for this data. [1]
(b) Use your table, assuming the masses are evenly spread within each class, to estimate the median mass. [2]
(c) Estimate the interquartile range. [2]
(d) Apples with a mass of more than 150 g are labelled 'large'. Estimate the number of large apples. [2]
ms: (b) A1: 129 g (129.3…; allow 128 to 130 from a graph)
(c) M1: LQ = 113.3 (20th value) and UQ = 145 (60th value)
(c) A1: 31.7 g (allow 30 to 33 from a graph)
questions.model:
(a) Cumulative frequencies: m ≤ 100: 8, m ≤ 120: 26, m ≤ 140: 56, m ≤ 160: 72, m ≤ 180: 80.
(b) Median = 40th value, in 120–140 (26 below it):
120 + (40 − 26)/30 × 20 = 120 + 9.33 = 129.3 g.
(c) LQ = 20th value: 100 + (20 − 8)/18 × 20 = 113.3 g.
UQ = 60th value: 140 + (60 − 56)/16 × 20 = 145 g.
IQR = 145 − 113.3 = 31.7 g.
(d) Half of the 140–160 class is above 150: 8 apples, plus 8 in 160–180, so about 16 large apples.
questions.tip: For 80 values use the 20th, 40th and 60th values for the quartiles and median.

questions.q:
(a) The number of goals scored by a team in each of its matches is shown.
Goals:      0 | 1 | 2 | 3
Frequency:  5 | x | 8 | 4
The mean number of goals is 1.44. Find the value of x. [3]
(b) In a test, the 12 students in class A have a mean mark of 64. The 18 students in class B have a mean mark of 59.
Calculate the mean mark of all 30 students. [2]
(c) For the same test, class A has median 62 and interquartile range 15. Class B has median 55 and interquartile range 28.
Make two comparisons between the marks of the two classes. [2]
ms: (c) B1: class A had a higher median, so on average class A did better
(c) B1: class B had a larger interquartile range, so class B's marks were more spread out (less consistent)
questions.model:
(a) Σfx = 0 × 5 + 1 × x + 2 × 8 + 3 × 4 = x + 28. Σf = 17 + x.
(x + 28) ÷ (17 + x) = 1.44
x + 28 = 24.48 + 1.44x → 3.52 = 0.44x → x = 8.
(b) Total marks = 12 × 64 + 18 × 59 = 768 + 1062 = 1830. Mean = 1830 ÷ 30 = 61.
(c) Class A has a higher median (62 > 55), so on average class A scored higher.
Class B has a larger IQR (28 > 15), so class B's marks were more spread out.
questions.tip: In comparisons, compare an average AND a measure of spread, and say what each means in context.
